en: The Sutra on the Great Meaning, translated by the Tripitaka Master Guṇabhadra of India during the Song Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with...
Together with twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus,
the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"In the past, there was a kingdom named Joyful and Free from Sorrow, and its king was called Vast Compassion."

In that country there was a householder named Mahādana, whose wife was named Candrā. They gave birth to a son of such upright and handsome appearance that he had few equals in the world; as soon as he fell to the ground, he spoke and made this vow:
"I shall practice giving throughout the world and rescue and deliver all people."
"Should there be those who are solitary, orphaned, or impoverished, I shall provide for and protect them so that they may attain peace and security.

Because of this, his parents named him Dṛḍhamati (Great Resolve). Seeing that he possessed extraordinary features unlike those of ordinary men, they feared he might be a deva, a nāga, or a spirit, and wished to perform divination to ascertain the truth.
The Great Being, having understood this, replied:
"I am indeed a human being, not a deva, nāga, ghost, or spirit.
I merely thought that those among the people of the world who are impoverished and in distress should be protected and cared for."
Having spoken these words, he ceased and said no more.
When he reached the age of seventeen, he addressed his parents, saying:
"I wish to practice giving, so that those who suffer may attain peace and security."
The parents thought to themselves,
"When our son was first born, he already made this vow.
They then said to their son:
"My wealth is immeasurable; I shall bestow it as I please, without any restriction.

Da Yi replied, "Although my parents' wealth is vast, it is still insufficient for my needs. I must enter the sea to gather the seven treasures in order to provide for and give to the people of the world."
After he had spoken thus several times, his parents finally consented and allowed him to go.
Da-yi then paid his respects, took his leave, and set out for the sea; on his way, he passed through another country.
In the kingdom there was a brāhmaṇa of immeasurable wealth who, seeing Mahāmati’s radiant countenance and upright features, took great delight in him and said:
"I hold you in high esteem; I have a young daughter whom I wish to offer to you. I pray that you will remain here."
Da Yi replied, "I have left my home to enter the sea to gather the seven treasures; I do not yet dare to grant you this request, as I must first return.

Thereupon, he proceeded and obtained the seven treasures, immediately dispatching a man to carry the jewels back to his native country, while he himself continued on to the edge of the sea to seek out other rare objects.

Suddenly he saw a great tree eighty *yojanas* high and eighty *yojanas* wide; Mahāmati then climbed the tree and from afar beheld a silver city, where the palaces, towers, and halls were all made of white silver, with celestial maidens attending by his side and music provided spontaneously.
There was a venomous snake that coiled itself three times around the city wall; upon seeing Dàyì, it raised its head to gaze at him. Dàyì thought to himself:
"That people are harmed by poison is solely due to a lack of benevolent intent."
He then sat down and focused his mind in meditative concentration; after a short while, the snake lowered its head and fell asleep.
As Dàyì was about to enter the city, the gatekeeper went in and informed the king, saying, "There is a worthy man outside who wishes to see the King."
The king himself went out to meet him and said with great joy,
"I only pray that you, O Benevolent One, will remain here for one season of three months, so that I may extend my offerings to you."
He replied, "I wish to go forth to gather treasures; it is not appropriate for me to remain here long.
The king responded:
“I shall not attend to state affairs; I only wish for you to remain here.
Thereupon, Mahāmaudgalyāyana stayed.

The king immediately provided him with clothing, food and drink, music, and bedding. When the ninety days had passed, Mahāmaudgalyāyana took his leave of the king, wishing to depart. The king then took various precious seven-jeweled treasures, intending to present them to him, but Mahāmaudgalyāyana said:
"I do not make much use of these seven treasures; however, I have heard that Your Majesty possesses a single bright moon pearl (candraprabha-maṇi), and I wish to seek it.
The king said, "I do not begrudge this pearl, but I fear only that the road is perilous and difficult, and thus I carry it with me myself."
Dàyì said: "When one is led by merit, a person does not fear hardships or perils.
The King said:
"This pearl is accompanied by treasures extending twenty li; I now offer it to you, sir, to do with as you wish.
Furthermore, if you later attain the Way, I pray that I may become your disciple and provide for your needs with even greater devotion than I do today."
Mahāmati then accepted the jewel and departed with joy.
Thereupon, Mahāmati proceeded further and saw a golden city.
Its palaces and halls were all made of gold; trees of the seven treasures produced music spontaneously, and the celestial maidens and attendants were twice as numerous as before.

There was also a venomous serpent that coiled six times around the city; upon seeing Dàyì, it raised its head to look at him, but when he again settled his mind in concentration, the serpent lowered its head and lay down.
As he intended to enter the city, the gatekeeper immediately went in and informed the king. The king then came out to welcome him and met with him, inviting him forward and saying:
"I pray that you will remain for a period of three months, so that we may extend our offerings to you."
Mahāmati then stayed behind; the king immediately received him with hospitality, providing him with food, drink, clothing, celestial maidens, and various musicians to entertain him.
After sixty days had passed, he took his leave of the king, wishing to depart. The king entreated him to remain, but his mind was not inclined to stay; thus, he bid the king farewell and left.
The king again presented him with rare and precious seven-jeweled treasures, but the Great Being refused them, saying:
"I have no desire for these various jewels. I hear that Your Majesty possesses a single 'bright moon' pearl (*candraprabha-maṇi*); I pray you, grant it to me."
The king said, "I do not dare begrudge it; I only fear that the road is far and perilous, and thus I am taking it with me. He replied:
"What difficulties or perils could there possibly be for one who dwells in the realm of merit? The King then replied:

"This pearl is surrounded by treasures extending forty li; I shall present it to you, O Benevolent One, so that after you have attained the Way, I may become your disciple. With spiritual powers beyond compare, I shall be able to offer you worship far exceeding what I do today."
He then joyfully accepted the pearl and departed.
Thereupon, Mahāmati proceeded further and again saw a city of crystal.
Its palaces and halls were all made of crystal; the trees of the seven treasures produced music spontaneously, and the celestial maidens in attendance were twice as numerous as before.
There was also a venomous snake that coiled nine times around the city wall; upon seeing Dàyì, it immediately raised its head to gaze at him.
Dàyì then sat down again, deeply reflecting and entering meditative concentration (*samādhi*), whereupon the snake lowered its head and fell back asleep.
When he intended to proceed, the gatekeeper entered and informed the king; the king immediately went out to welcome him and invited him forward, saying:
"I pray that you will stay for a period of three months."
Mahāmati then remained.

The king again provided him with offerings to the full extent of his means, furnishing food, drink, clothing, and music to entertain him; after forty days had passed, he once more took leave of the king and departed.
The king then took various rare and precious seven-jeweled treasures, intending to present them to him; however, Mahātyāga would not accept them and replied, "I have no need for these many jewels.
I have heard that the king possesses a single moon-bright pearl; I wish for you to grant it to me."
The King then replied:

"This pearl is pursued by treasures from within sixty *li*; I now offer it to you, O Benevolent One. If you later attain the Way, I pray that you will take me as your disciple; your wisdom shall be peerless, and I shall provide for you with offerings even greater than those of today."
He then accepted the pearl with joy and departed.
Thereupon, Mahāmati proceeded further and again saw a city of lapis lazuli.
Its palaces and halls were all made of lapis lazuli; the trees of the seven treasures produced music spontaneously, and the celestial maidens serving as attendants were twice as numerous as before.

He also saw a venomous snake coil itself twelve times around the city; upon seeing Mahāmaudgalyāyana, it raised its head to look at him. As soon as Mahāmaudgalyāyana sat down again and entered deep meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the snake lowered its head and fell back asleep.

When Mahāmati was about to depart, the gatekeeper entered and informed the king; the king came out to welcome him and requested that he stay for one month or three months, whereupon Mahāmati remained.
The king personally provided him with offerings of food, drink, clothing, and music for his entertainment; after twenty days had passed, he took his leave of the king, wishing to depart.
The king immediately took exquisite seven-jeweled treasures to present to him, but Mahādeva would not accept these precious gems, saying:
"I have heard that Your Majesty possesses a single 'bright moon' pearl; I pray you grant it to me."
The King replied:

"This pearl is worth eighty *li* of rare treasures; I shall offer it to you, O Benevolent One. I pray that when you later attain the Way, I may become your disciple and provide pure-minded offerings exceeding those of today, so that I may long obtain wisdom."
Mahāmati then accepted the jewels and departed with joy.
Mahāmati thought to himself:
"I originally came seeking treasures; now my wish is fulfilled, and I shall return from here."
He then sought out the old path, intending to return to his native land, and traveled across the great ocean. Thereupon, the various divine kings within the sea deliberated together, saying:
"Although there are many rare and famous treasures in our sea, we have no pearls such as these."
He then commanded the Sea God to seize the pearl by force.
The god immediately transformed himself into a human being and met with Dàyì, asking him:
"I have heard that you have obtained a rare and extraordinary object; might I borrow it for a moment to see it?"
Dàyì reached out his hand and showed him the four pearls; the Sea God then shook his hand, causing the pearls to fall into the water.
Dàyì thought to himself:
"When the King spoke with me, he said only that these pearls were difficult to preserve."
"I have fortunately already obtained it, yet now it has been snatched away by this son; this is not right.
He then addressed the sea deity, saying:

"I personally underwent diligent toil and traversed perilous terrain to obtain this pearl. You, on the contrary, have snatched it from me; if you do not return it now, I shall drain the waters of the ocean dry."
The sea deity, knowing this, asked:
"How lofty is your resolve?
The ocean is three million three hundred and sixty thousand yojanas deep and its breadth is boundless; how can you possibly exhaust it?"
For example, the sun will never fall to the earth, nor can a great wind be grasped or bound;
though the sun might be made to fall to the earth and the wind might be grasped and bound, the waters of the great ocean can never be bailed out until they are exhausted.
Daiyi smiled and replied to him, saying:

"I have reflected that the bones accumulated from my successive births and deaths throughout the cycle of saṃsāra exceed Mount Sumeru in height; the blood that has flowed would not be matched even by the five rivers and four seas."
"I still desire to sever the very root of this cycle of birth and death; yet, why should this small sea not be drained?
He further spoke, saying:
"I recall that in the past, when making offerings to the various Buddhas, I made a vow, saying:"
"May my aspirations and conduct be courageous in the Way, so that I encounter no difficulty in whatever direction I turn.
Even if Mount Sumeru were moved and the waters of the great ocean were exhausted, I shall never retreat from my resolve."
He then unified his mind and began to bale out the seawater with a vessel.
The resonance of his sincerity reached the first of the four heavens, where the King descended to assist Mahāmati in baling the water; in three parts, he had already baled out two.
Thereupon, all the various kings and spirits of the ocean were greatly terrified and deliberated together, saying:
"If we do not return this pearl now, it will not be a minor matter; the waters will dry up and the mud will be exposed, and you will then destroy our palaces."
The sea deity then brought forth various treasures to give to Da Yi, but Da Yi would not accept them, declaring:
"I have no need for these things; I desire only my own pearl. Return my pearl to me at once, for I will by no means let you keep it."
The sea deity, perceiving his sincere devotion, brought forth the pearl and returned it to him.
Having obtained the pearl, Mahādeva took a Brahmin girl as his wife and returned to his native country, where he practiced great acts of charity according to his heart’s desire.

From that time forward, within his realm there were no longer any who suffered from hunger, cold, or destitution; people from all directions abandoned their former lands to come under his benevolent rule, carrying even infants in swaddling clothes.

Thus he practiced giving for many years, so that his grace reached even the smallest creatures—whether flying insects, crawling beasts, or wriggling worms—none of whom failed to receive its nourishment.
Thereafter, when his life ended, he ascended to become Śakra Devānām Indra, or descended to become a Cakravartin Emperor.
By accumulating merit, he attained Buddhahood for himself and became the uniquely honored one within the three realms; all of this resulted from his past conduct and was not spontaneous.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The one named Great Intention was my own self;
the householder Mahādhana at that time is the present King Śuddhodana."
The mother Candā at that time was the present Queen Māyā;
the King of the Joyful and Sorrowless Country at that time was Mahākāśyapa;
and the Brahmin girl at that time was Kūṭadantī.
The father of the girl at that time was Maitreya;
the king in the city of silver at that time was Ānanda;
and the king in the city of gold at that time was Maudgalyāyana.
The king who ruled the city of Crystal at that time was Śāriputra;
the king who ruled the city of Lapis Lazuli at that time was the bhikṣu Sūta;
and the fourth heavenly king who assisted Mahāmati in bailing out the ocean was none other than Udāyin.
He who at that time seized the jewel was none other than Devadatta;
those who were the guardians of the four city gates were Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, Svāgata, and Kṛṣṇa;
and those who were the poisonous snakes circling the four cities were the four ministers who conspired to kill Aṅgulimāla.
Ānanda adjusted his robes, prostrated, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"At that time, by what merit did Mahāmati bring about these four precious cities, so that he received offerings everywhere?"
"And how did he obtain the four bright moon-jewels?
All manner of treasures followed after them. The Buddha said:

"In the past, during the era of the Buddha Vipaśyin, Da Yi once constructed a stupa for the Buddha using four precious substances and made offerings to the Triple Gem while observing the eightfold fast for seven days.

At that time, five hundred people simultaneously established monasteries together—some hanging silk banners and lighting lamps, some burning incense and scattering flowers, some making offerings to the bhikṣu-saṃgha, and some reciting sutras and expounding the Way—and they have all come to this assembly today."
Ānanda and the fourfold assembly of disciples, having heard the sutra, rejoiced and came forward to pay homage to the Buddha.
This concludes the *Mahāyāna-sūtra*.
